title: The text itself
hookLine: scholars also test whether the text fits the Qur'an and known sunnah

cards: Aisha has just heard a report that troubles her. It came through people she respects: Umar, and his son Abdullah. It says a dead person is punished because their family weeps over them.
Someone in the grave, punished for a grieving mother's tears? Aisha doesn't attack the men who carried it. She goes to the words themselves, and to the Qur'an.
You've met this scene before, with Aisha the scholar. Today, look at what it shows: a hadith's text being weighed, not just its chain. Today, the matn.

teach.b: Matn is the text of a hadith, the part after the names: what was actually said or done. The chain asks who carried it. The matn asks: does this fit?
Aisha's test, in Bukhari, is, in effect: may Allah have mercy on Umar, but the Prophet ﷺ didn't say that about a believer.
He said it about a man who rejected faith, whose punishment was being increased while his family wept.

Then she reaches for the Qur'an: enough for you is the Book, which says no soul carries another's load. In the version in Sahih Muslim she adds something gentle. The men who reported it weren't liars, she says.

But hearing can slip. That's the whole idea in one breath: an honest chain can still carry a misheard sentence, so the words get tested on their own. Later scholars didn't simply throw one report away.

They asked how the reports fit together. Al-Bukhari's own chapter heading reads the saying narrowly: it applies, he suggests, when wailing had been the dead person's own custom. Others reconciled it in other ways.

And a careful reader asks of any text: does it clash with the Qur'an? With sunnah that's well established? Does it promise a mountain of reward for a tiny act, or speak in a way that doesn't sound like him at all?
Later scholars, such as Ibn al-Qayyim, gathered signs like these in their books. The chain gets a report through the door. The text still has to sit at the table with everything else that's known.

how: Hadith scholars examine a report's text as well as its chain, asking whether it agrees with the Qur'an, with well-established sunnah and with other reports, and they discuss how apparently conflicting reports fit together.

s: once a chain is sound, the text is never questioned
Aisha questioned a report carried by people she trusted, by weighing its words.
Aisha called the men who carried the report liars
in Muslim's version she says they weren't liars, but hearing can slip.
scholars also tried to fit apparently conflicting reports together
al-Bukhari's chapter heading reads the saying narrowly instead of discarding it.

games.q: you're Aisha. a trusted man reports a saying that seems to clash with the Qur'an. what do you do?
o: accept it; the man is honest.
go to the words and weigh them against the Qur'an.
games.why: she weighed the words against the Qur'an, and said the men weren't liars, but hearing can slip.

practice: Find a quote you've seen lately with a well-known name on it: a poster line, a caption, something forwarded with a picture of a scholar or a saint or a president.
Set the name aside and look only at the words: does it sound like the rest of what that person said, does it promise too much, does it clash with what they stood for?
You don't need a verdict; just ask Aisha's questions, slowly, of one sentence.
